title: Ambedkar's conversion
hookLine: at Nagpur, Dr B. R. Ambedkar and a great crowd of Dalits take refuge

cards: An open ground in Nagpur, a city in the middle of India, and a great crowd stretching back across it.
In the crowd are Dalits, people the caste system had called untouchable: kept from common wells, from temple doors, from classrooms. At the front stands a lawyer and scholar, Dr. B.
R. Ambedkar, who helped version the constitution of independent India and spent his life fighting caste discrimination. Today he isn't here to argue a case.
He's here to take refuge in the Buddha.

teach.h: BORN DALIT, KEPT FROM THE WATER.
teach.b: First, his own life. Ambedkar was born into a Dalit family. Accounts of his childhood say he had to sit apart at school and couldn't drink from the common water unless someone poured it for him.
He studied anyway, in India and abroad, and became a lawyer, an economist and a leader of his people.

teach.h: A LONG SEARCH, HIS OWN REASONS.
teach.b: Second, a long search. Long before this day, he had said publicly that he would leave the religion he was born into, and he studied more than one path before choosing.
He chose the Buddha's, for his own reasons: a teaching that, as he read it, rested on reason, compassion and the equal worth of every person. This is his story and his reading, told here as his.
Hindus have their own and varied answers to caste, and Hindu reformers have fought untouchability too. Third, the ceremony.
Accounts say Ambedkar first received the refuges and precepts himself from a senior Buddhist monk.

teach.h: HE TAKES REFUGE, THEN LEADS IT.
teach.b: Then he turned to the crowd and led them through the refuges in Pali, line by line: Buddham saranam gacchami, I go to the Buddha for refuge; then the Dhamma; then the Sangha. A whole field of voices repeating after one.
Fourth, the week. Chiyono's bucket, the water gone and the moon still in the sky. Ledi Sayadaw opening meditation to everyone.

Mahasi's rising, falling. Ajahn Mun in the forests, Ajahn Chah at the gate, Buddhadasa's plain words. And today, on an open ground, a crowd that had been refused dignity for generations stands up and chooses it.

how: Ambedkarite Buddhists mark the anniversary of the Nagpur conversion each year, and crowds gather at the site in Nagpur, now called Deekshabhoomi, to take the refuges and remember Ambedkar.

games.q: you're Ambedkar at Nagpur. you've just received the refuges from a senior monk. the crowd is waiting. what do you do?
o: let the monks receive each person one by one.
turn and lead the whole crowd through the refuges yourself.

games.why: accounts say he turned to the crowd and led them through the refuges himself, so their refuge came through one of their own.

practice: Bring to mind someone, from your family, your history or your neighborhood, who had to fight to be treated as fully human: to learn, to vote, to be served, to be heard. Hold their face or their name for a few breaths.
You don't need to say anything; just let them be honored for a moment, here, in you.

wordCard.voice: Ambedkar's conversion. At Nagpur, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar takes refuge in the Buddha, then leads a great crowd of Dalits through the refuges. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: I go to the Buddha for refuge. the first of the three refuges Ambedkar led the crowd through.

carryVoice: Your line: dignity chosen. Refuge, taken together by a whole field of voices. Until tomorrow.
